When Sonnet 4.5 was released back in 2025, we saw the model exhibit a behavior that came to be known as "context anxiety": as it approached its context window limit, it would wrap work up early and stop with room to spare. To compensate for this behavior, we spent time and energy building in context resets into our agent harnesses. But when Opus 4.5 shipped, the model stopped showing this behavior entirely, so the harness fixes we built in turned into pure overhead. Harnesses encodes assumptions about what the model cannot do on its own today, and those assumptions go stale as models improve. Check out our talk that Gagan Bhat and I gave at AI Engineer World's Fair, where we discuss the lessons we learned building harnesses that adapt alongside models: https://lnkd.in/gdX4xbXt Huge shoutout to AI Engineer for hosting an amazing conference - what a fun crowd to present to!

Prodigy has already achieved over 100% returns in live trading over the course of the YC S26 batch, while major indices like the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were down or flat. Their model beats Claude Fable and GPT-5.6 Sol at financial and quant research benchmarks. Prodigy's strategies are delta-neutral, and thanks to rigorous and comprehensive risk controls, they've never had a down week. Trading firms generated hundreds of billions in profit last year, and this number is growing quickly YoY. Jane Street alone is on track for a $64 billion run rate in 2026. Global equities markets now exceed $150 trillion in capitalization. Prodigy's models find new opportunities and alpha in the financial markets faster than any team of human quant researchers. The founders, Michael W. and Yuhua W. , are brothers who left seven-figure jobs to build the future of quant trading. They bring together over 16 years of combined experience in quantitative finance, frontier model research, and large-scale AI infrastructure. Michael was a senior researcher at Google DeepMind, where he trained SoTA foundation models. He previously worked as a quant and Series 57-licensed securities trader at Jane Street, where he built strategies that generated billions in PnL, growing a small desk to one of the most profitable in the whole firm. Yuhua built cutting-edge AI at Apple, serving billions of users across the world. A new era has arrived in the world of quantitative finance. To learn more, contact founders@prodigy.markets . Our paper "XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System" received the Test of Time Award at #KDD2026 ! The honor belongs to the entire community that made #XGBoost project today. Especially the maintainers Hyunsu Cho , Rory Mitchell , jiaming yuan Nan Zhu and others who continues to make the project awesome for the entire community. This is also special for me personally, as KDD is where my research career began through the KDD Cup, sparking my journey into ML systems research. In retrospect, it is hard to predict whether one's work will stand the test of time, but one can always make sure it passes the test of passion, dedication, and courage. That experience still carries me today, and hopefully continues to serve as a gift for the future. I will be giving a talk tomorrow at the award session on the paper, history, and lessons learned.

I spent this summer working at Texas Instruments in Dallas, TX as an AI Solutions Engineer Intern on the AI for Personalization team. Nearly everything I worked on touched the recommender system on TI.com , which surfaces related electrical components while an engineer is browsing a part. My main project was a Thompson Sampling multi-armed bandit for per-company personalization, so an engineer's recommendations draw on their whole company's design context, not just their own browsing. I also shipped a new email recommendations channel, with its own logic built on customers' order and browsing history, now running around 400 campaigns a day. Outside my core work, the highlight was the ITS Innovation Week hackathon, where I built the RAG system for our agentic project that auto-generates testbenches from a netlist and spec. The kind of thing that takes an engineer hours, reduced to minutes. Coming in, I didn't know much about electrical engineering. Leaving, I still don't know much about electrical engineering, but I got to see firsthand how ML gets applied in a domain where the products are physical, the customers are engineers, and the stakes are real hardware decisions. Back to Pittsburgh for my final year at CMU.
